Experiment · 12–15 Oct 2026 · rig-annotations branch

Rig Judge Model Trial

Can a fast decision model look at a rendered rig and tell us whether the parts are stitched correctly, and which way to nudge a part that isn't? Three System One models (Cloudflare's Clef Flash and Clef 27B, and TypeSafe's Jev 1.14) got the same images and the same questions in seven tests: planted defects, joint close-ups, the frames your reviewer rejected, and three generations of each rig.

Spot the real rejects, one frame at a timeJev, clearly

Full-body rejects vs their fixes: AUROC 0.99 for Jev, 0.76 for 27B and 0.73 for Flash.

Flag a displaced joint in a close-upJev and 27B, with the master

On the audited labels: Jev 0.82, 27B 0.78, Flash 0.66. Larger shifts are caught more often.

Say which way to move the partNot yet, any model

Direction answers sit near chance in every condition, and Jev's Box edges are as coarse as the shifts. Leave nudges to code.

Ground truth · read this before the joint-crop numbers

The approved rig isn't perfectly clean

The 183 "clean" joint crops are only 15 distinct images (one per joint of the approved setup pose), each repeated 6–20 times. Four of them are the hands, which don't match the master: the glove fit and the wrist trim are what took the most fix rounds (T17b to M2). Those four make up 62 of the 183 negatives, and they're where Jev and 27B score highest. So every joint-crop test is reported twice: as labelled, and audited, with those four joints taken out of the clean set (they stay as positives when shifted). The real reviewed frames and the rig-generation tests don't depend on this audit.

Test 1 · full frame

A whole frame with one planted defect

Asked of a ~520×720 render: Does the frame show a rigging or stitching defect?, plus kind, part, side, direction and size. 120 frames from the approved rigs: 38 clean; 82 with one part shifted 3–24 px, a sleeve over the torso, a tail in front, or a mirrored hand.

What the models saw, and what they said

The magenta box marks the planted change for this page; the models got the plain image. None of the three can tell these frames apart: a 3–24 px shift at this scale is a handful of pixels on a 520 px figure.

Tests 2 and 3 · joint close-ups

One joint, cropped where the rig says it is

Setup pose. Each crop is a square centred on a bone's attachment point (wrist, neck, waist, ankle, tail and antler roots), rendered at 2× so render and master are equally sharp. 363 crops: 180 with that joint's part shifted 8, 16 or 24 px in one of four directions. Two questions: Is the part displaced from its joint? and Which way has it moved?. Test 2 sends the render crop alone; Test 3 also sends the same square cut from the approved master.

Test 4 · new · joint close-up against the previous render

Did this fix round move the part, and which way?

The fix-loop question. The same joint crop from the approved render (before) and from the shifted render (after), cut at exactly the same place, so both sides have exact ground truth and the master's own differences are out of the picture. 180 shifted crops, plus the 15 clean joints shown against themselves as a check.

Even with a perfectly clean reference, no model gives a usable fix direction. Each has a favourite answer it gives whatever the shift. Detecting that something moved works much better than saying which way.

Test 7 · Jev only · the new Box question

Box: where is the part?

Box takes a target description (the hand that comes out of the sleeve cuff in `render`) and returns four edges as fractions of the image, plus a confidence. Neither Clef model has an equivalent. Ground truth for render crops is exact (the part's rig layer). On master crops there's no exact box, so the master boxes are checked against your hand-placed wrist and fingertip landmarks instead.

Confidence runs only 0.02–0.13. Its rank correlation with box quality is 0.33 on the render alone and 0.00 with the master. Treat it as a weak ranking signal, not a probability.

Box finds the part well enough to choose where to crop or what to inspect. Its edges are off by about as much as the shifts move them, so subtracting two boxes can't read an 8–24 px offset yet. The two-pass close-up changed mean IoU from 0.49 to 0.48. On full frames, the box for "the part that looks wrong" landed on the planted change 20% of the time; a random point lands there about 7%.

What this means

Where a model earns a place in the pipeline

A reject screen before human review

Jev, one frame at a time, on full-body frames. It separates real rejects from fixes and ranks older builds below approved ones. Calibrate a threshold per character on more rounds, then let it flag frames for review.

≈ $0.0001 per frame

A joint check with the master beside it

Jev or 27B on master + render crops at each joint. Useful for gaps at hands and boots. Clean up the approved set's hand joints first, or they read as permanent false alarms.

≈ 1.8k tokens per joint

Keep nudges in code

Direction is at chance for all three models, and two boxes can't resolve 8–24 px. Align each part's own mask to the master or the previous render. That's exact.

no model cost

Use Box to aim, not to measure

Box finds the part (IoU about 0.5–0.6; master hand boxes cover your wrist and fingertip landmarks 79% of the time). Good for choosing where to crop or what to inspect next.

Jev only
Raw answers, labels and scripts: experiments/2026-10-12-clef-judge/. No pipeline code was changed. Every number on this page is computed from the saved result files.
